sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: Each turn names the prior speaker, e.g. T4 answers the Existentialist's absurdity claim.
sub.limitation: Mostly just restates the prior claim, then pivots to its own position.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: T4 says an existential sermon is as tedious as a moral lesson.
sub.limitation: T8 and T9 repeat the warmth-versus-rawness split from T5 and T6 with nothing new.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: T8 and T9 pit warmth of connection against stark, liberated hope.
sub.limitation: The core question, how hope arrives without a lesson, gets only a passing look.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: In T7 the Aestheticist concedes that pure beauty was too narrow.
sub.limitation: The concession comes without a stated cause and changes no one else's view.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: In T9 the choice comes down to comfort versus challenge.
sub.limitation: The user ends with a single title and an abstract binary.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: T2 accurately restates the Aestheticist's 'beauty is enough' before qualifying it.
sub.limitation: In T8 the Existentialist position shrinks to 'raw tension' that obscures warmth.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: T4 makes a real point: existential struggle can turn into its own sermon.
sub.limitation: T6's 'too smooth' objection is asserted without saying why smoothness kills hope.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: T1 quotes 'all art is quite useless' accurately, with pd=true.
sub.limitation: T7's 'mirror to the world' reverses the Preface, which says art mirrors the spectator.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: Turns hedge suitably with 'perhaps' and 'might'.
sub.limitation: Calling Forster 'The Structuralist' is an anachronistic label presented as a description.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: T7 is an explicit concession, and T9 leaves the dispute open honestly.
sub.limitation: No reason is given for the T7 reversal, so it reads as convenience.

sub.name: Identification of actual concern
sub.example: Section A names the uncertainty between artistic form and existential ambiguity.
sub.limitation: It never asks what 'obvious life lessons' has meant in the user's reading so far.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: T5 links 'short' and 'without obvious lesson' to A Room with a View.
sub.limitation: The 'short' constraint barely shapes the rest of the argument.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: T2 respects the user's wish not to be preached to.
sub.limitation: T6 steers toward a 'difficult work', drifting from the hope the user asked for.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: T6 proposes a two-chapter trial, which suits a modest commitment.
sub.limitation: Length and mood constraints are never weighed directly.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: Section E branches on warmth versus intellectual clarity.
sub.limitation: There are no focused questions about the user's past reading or taste.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: T8 suggests the user might 'actually be craving' human warmth, offered tentatively.
sub.limitation: Motives stay generic and are never tied to what the user wrote.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: T4 exposes the hidden assumption that only moral lessons are didactic.
sub.limitation: It never asks what 'hopeful' assumes about how a book should end.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: Section D asks: comfort you, or challenge your perspective?
sub.limitation: This values split is stated but not explored through cases.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: T3 touches on suspicion of 'false, comforting conclusions'.
sub.limitation: It never examines why lessons put the user off, e.g. a fear of being condescended to.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: Section E's page-comparison test leaves the user to judge the tone.
sub.limitation: The distinctions are broad and hard to refine or reject usefully.

sub.name: Definition of decision and options
sub.example: T5 names A Room with a View as a concrete option.
sub.limitation: Only one title is named, and the 'short, difficult work' in T6 is never specified.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: T8 says rawness can obscure warmth.
sub.limitation: The tradeoffs are abstract, not set against particular books.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: Section E: prioritise warmth, choose character-driven; prioritise courage, choose existential.
sub.limitation: The conditions are generic categories, not tied to observable preferences.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: Section A names one decisive uncertainty.
sub.limitation: It doesn't separate key unknowns (tolerance for sadness) from minor ones.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: T6 suggests reading two chapters; Section E suggests comparing a few pages.
sub.limitation: With no titles attached, the steps are hard to act on.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: Plain, readable sentences throughout, e.g. T2.
sub.limitation: 'Absurdity of your situation' in T3 is jargon applied to a book request.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: Every turn names whom it answers.
sub.limitation: T6's 'short, difficult work' gives the reader no referent.

sub.name: Manageable pacing
sub.example: Nine brief turns stay within the 25–65 word limit.
sub.limitation: The turns are short enough that some arguments feel truncated.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions
sub.example: Beauty, character and absurdity are three clear stances.
sub.limitation: The voices sound alike, and the 'Structuralist' label confuses Forster's stance.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: No long recaps inside the debate.
sub.limitation: Section D repeats T9's binary almost word for word.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: T8 frames a real choice: warmth or rawness.
sub.limitation: Stakes are low, and nothing about the user's reading life is at risk.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: T7 has the Aestheticist reverse on pure beauty.
sub.limitation: The reversal has no trigger, so it doesn't land.

sub.name: Personality and voice
sub.example: T1 echoes Wilde's paradoxical flair.
sub.limitation: Forster and Camus sound like interchangeable moderators.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: T4's line: a sermon on existence is as tedious as a moral lesson.
sub.limitation: There are no vivid examples or analogies from actual novels.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: The T7 concession briefly shifts the dynamic.
sub.limitation: The rhythm is flat and every turn has the same cadence.

strengths: T1 quotes Wilde accurately with pd=true, and the form rules are respected.
T4's point that existential struggle can become its own sermon is genuinely sharp.
Section E offers a usable comparison test that leaves the user to judge.
weaknesses: Only one title is offered (T5), and T6's 'short, difficult work' is never named.
T7's Aestheticist inverts Wilde's mirror line and concedes with no stated reason.
The Existentialist (T6) steers away from the hope the user explicitly asked for.
editorNotes: When the user asks 'what might suit me', require at least three specific titles tied to the minds' arguments.
Require each concession to name the specific argument that caused it.
Forbid anachronistic role titles; role labels must fit the author's own era and stance.
Have at least one turn ask a focused question about the user's past reading.

sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: T6 picks up T5's 'your labor' and turns it toward self-deception.
sub.limitation: T8 skips past T7's revision and jumps straight to a test.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: T7 moves from ambiguity to precise, short structure that prevents projection.
sub.limitation: The Reader-Response position barely develops after T2.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: T3, T6 and T9 probe hope as understanding versus retreat into sentiment.
sub.limitation: Whether a hopeful book can avoid sentimentality is assumed doubtful rather than tested.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: In T7 the Formalist revises after the Ethicist's projection objection.
sub.limitation: The Reader-Response Critic never absorbs the Ethicist's challenge.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: T9 sharpens the question: clearer perception of others, or a warmer self-feeling?
sub.limitation: The sharper question moves the user further from an actual book choice.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: T4 restates the Ethicist's self-deception worry fairly before countering.
sub.limitation: T2's 'the book holds all the weight' overstates T1's Formalist claim.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: T6 tests whether the user's labour can be merely self-confirming.
sub.limitation: T5's 'regardless of whether the final tone is…hopeful' sidesteps the user's stated goal.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: The gaps (Iser), unselfing (Murdoch) and anti-pamphlet (Kundera) views are fairly represented.
sub.limitation: T8's 'gaps in her narration': Brodie is not the narrator, and hopefulness is doubtful.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: T6 frames the defence-mechanism idea as a question, not a fact.
sub.limitation: T1's 'ceases to be a novel and becomes a pamphlet' overstates a preference as fact.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: T7: 'I drop my earlier claim' and gives the Ethicist's reason.
sub.limitation: The Ethicist never concedes that wanting hope can be legitimate.

sub.name: Identification of actual concern
sub.example: Section A flags the risk of choosing sentimentality over complexity.
sub.limitation: It reframes the request as suspect rather than clarifying it.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: T7 uses 'short' as an argument: brevity forces an encounter with the real.
sub.limitation: 'Thoughtful' and the dislike of lessons are treated abstractly.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: T1 honours the dislike of obvious lessons.
sub.limitation: T3 and T6 treat the stated wish for hope as a likely self-deception.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: T8's 30 pages in one sitting suits a short-novel reader.
sub.limitation: It ignores the mood constraint by suggesting a dark novel.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: T9: 'That fact is the detail only you can provide.'
sub.limitation: There is no direct question about past books that felt hopeful or preachy.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: T9 separates hope as achieved understanding from hope as retreat.
sub.limitation: T6's 'defense mechanism' edges toward declaring a hidden motive.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: T2 questions the assumption that hope lives in the text, not the reader.
sub.limitation: The Ethicist's own assumption that hope-seeking is suspect goes unexamined.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: Section E weighs challenge, agency and self-discovery as distinct priorities.
sub.limitation: It doesn't show where these values actually conflict in a book choice.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: T3 names the fear of mistaking false sentiment for insight.
sub.limitation: T6's 'comforted by a lie' tips into pathologising an ordinary wish.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: T8's reading test lets the user check the claims against their own experience.
sub.limitation: The framing pressures toward the Ethicist's answer instead of leaving it open.

sub.name: Definition of decision and options
sub.example: T8 names The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie.
sub.limitation: One title, poorly matched to 'hopeful'; there are no alternatives.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: T4 sets ambiguity against neat endings as two kinds of hope.
sub.limitation: No option's cost is spelled out in reading terms.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: Section E maps value-challenge, agency and self-discovery to book types.
sub.limitation: The categories ('significant narrative gaps') are hard to apply when browsing.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: T9 names the unknown the user must supply.
sub.limitation: It doesn't rank this unknown against simpler ones like tolerance for sad endings.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: T8's 30-page sitting is a limited, concrete trial.
sub.limitation: The trial book may well fail the user's hope criterion.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: T1 ('pamphlet') and T6 ('comforted by a lie') are crisp.
sub.limitation: 'Fill the gaps' and 'encounter with the real' in T2 and T7 are unexplained theory jargon.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: T4–T7 each name the claim they answer.
sub.limitation: The basis lines give no chapters or links, so they're hard to trace.

sub.name: Manageable pacing
sub.example: Turns run 45–60 words with a steady exchange.
sub.limitation: Dense turns stack abstractions without examples.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions
sub.example: Text, reader and ethics positions are clearly distinct; T7 marks its change explicitly.
sub.limitation: T8 abandons the debate thread for a recommendation without linking back.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: Little repetition inside the debate.
sub.limitation: Section D re-explains T9's dichotomy at length.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: T6 raises real stakes: whether the user's hope is honest.
sub.limitation: The stakes come partly from suspicion of the user, not the issue.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: T7's Formalist reversal follows plausibly from T6.
sub.limitation: T8's swerve to Spark is abrupt rather than surprising.

sub.name: Personality and voice
sub.example: The Ethicist's austere, probing voice fits Murdoch.
sub.limitation: Kundera's irony and Iser's play barely come through.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: T1: 'ceases to be a novel and becomes a pamphlet.'
sub.limitation: There are no vivid scenes or examples from actual novels.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: Tension builds from T3 to T6, then T7 releases it.
sub.limitation: The tone stays uniformly severe, at odds with a hopeful brief.

strengths: T7 makes a genuine, reasoned revision prompted by T6's projection objection.
The debate sharpens a real question: hope as understanding versus self-soothing (T9).
It keeps to the form: no quotation marks, pd flags honest, turns within word limits.
weaknesses: Only one recommendation (T8, Brodie), poorly fitted to 'hopeful', and 'her narration' is inaccurate.
The Ethicist (T3, T6) treats the user's wish for hope as suspect, edging into pathologising.
The basis lines give no chapter or link, so grounding is hard to check.
editorNotes: For recommendation requests, require three or more specific titles, each checked against the user's stated mood goal.
Tell the minds to take the user's stated wish as legitimate and question its shape, not its validity.
Require chapter-level basis references for every turn.
Have one turn ground an abstract claim in a concrete scene from a named novel.
